summary: Describes a pseudowire encapsulation for TDM bit-streams such as T1, E1, T3 and E3 that ignores any structure the standard TDM framing imposes on the stream. This lets old telephone-style circuits be carried across packet networks. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Old phone lines send a steady stream of bits. This packs that stream into ordinary internet-style packets without trying to understand it, like putting a hose of water into buckets.

questions: how does satop carry t1 and e1
subtitle: Carrying T1, E1, T3 and E3 bit-streams across a packet network as pseudowires, without interpreting their framing.

tldr.problem: Circuits such as T1, E1, T3 and E3 need to be carried across packet-switching networks, often between provider edges that have no need to interpret the TDM data.
tldr.mechanism: SAToP chops the bit-stream into fixed-size payloads, adds a 4-byte control word (with sequence number and fault flags) and an optional RTP header, and sends the result through a UDP, L2TPv3 or MPLS pseudowire.
tldr.outcome: The emulated circuit is sensitive to packet loss and SAToP itself provides no protection against network outages. Structure-aware alternatives are noted for hiding packet loss from the customer.

today: RFC 4553 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What SAToP Does
sections.content:
SAToP, Structure-Agnostic TDM over Packet, is a method for encapsulating Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) bit-streams (T1, E1, T3, E3) as pseudowires over packet-switching networks (PSN). It completely disregards any structure imposed on these signals, in particular standard TDM framing. This fits cases where the provider edges (PEs) do not need to interpret TDM data or take part in TDM signaling.

The services emulated are E1 (2048 kbit/s), T1 (1544 kbit/s, also known as DS1), E3 (34368 kbit/s) and T3 (44736 kbit/s, also known as DS3). How the circuit reaches the PE does not matter: a T1 is treated the same whether it arrives on copper, inside a T3, or in a SONET/SDH virtual tributary.

SAToP conforms to the PWE3 architecture of RFC 3985 and the requirements of RFC 4197. Pseudowires may be configured manually or set up with the PWE3 control protocol of RFC 4447.
sections.plainLanguage: SAToP carries old phone-style signals over modern networks without peeking inside them, like a courier delivering sealed boxes.

sections.title: Packet Layout and Control Word
sections.content:
A SAToP packet is made of PSN and pseudowire demultiplexing headers, the SAToP header and the TDM payload. UDP or L2TPv3 can provide demultiplexing over an IPv4/IPv6 PSN, and the PW label does so over MPLS. The packet MUST NOT exceed the path MTU, and IPv4 implementations MUST set Don't Fragment.

The SAToP header MUST contain a 4-byte control word and MAY contain a fixed RTP header. The RTP header follows the control word, except with UDP multiplexing where it precedes it. The control word holds four zero bits, then:

  • L: set when the payload is invalid because of an attachment circuit fault; the payload MAY then be omitted.
  • R: set by the PSN-bound side when its local CE-bound side is in the packet loss state.
  • RSV and FRG (bits 6 to 9): set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.
  • LEN (bits 10 to 15): MAY carry the packet length if under 64 bytes, otherwise zero.
  • Sequence number: 16 bits, random initial value, incremented with each packet.

When RTP is used, the P, X, CC and M fields MUST be zero, the payload type comes from the dynamic range, and the timestamp clock MUST be an integer multiple of 8 kHz, with 8 kHz mandatory to support. Absolute mode timestamps from the recovered TDM clock and MUST be supported with RTP. Differential mode uses a common timing source and is OPTIONAL.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bucket gets a small label saying its number, whether the water in it is bad, and whether the sender has been missing buckets lately.

sections.title: Payload Sizes and Octet-Aligned T1
sections.content:
Every packet in a given pseudowire carries a fixed number of bytes of TDM data. The size is set at setup, is the same in both directions and stays unchanged for the life of the pseudowire. Bits fill each byte from most significant to least significant. All implementations MUST be able to support these payload sizes: E1 256 bytes, T1 192 bytes, and E3 and T3 1024 bytes. No alignment to TDM frames is assumed.

An optional octet-aligned T1 mode exists for T1 circuits already padded to whole bytes. The payload is a number of 25-byte subframes, each carrying 193 bits of TDM data and 7 bits of padding. Implementations that support it MUST support a payload of 200 bytes, which is precisely 1 millisecond of TDM data. This mode does not interoperate with the non-aligned T1 mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Every bucket holds exactly the same amount, so if one is lost the receiver knows exactly how much is missing.

sections.title: How the Interworking Function Behaves
sections.content:
The interworking function (IWF) packetizes TDM data going toward the PSN, adds the SAToP, demultiplexing and PSN headers, and transmits. In the other direction, the CE-bound IWF SHOULD use a jitter buffer whose size is locally configurable, and SHOULD use sequence numbers to detect lost and misordered packets. Misordered packets that cannot be reordered MUST be discarded and treated as lost.

Lost packets are replaced with replacement data, which defaults to the "all ones" pattern, and packets with the L bit set are likewise replaced with all ones. Before setup and after teardown the IWF plays all ones. After setup it stays in an intermediate state, still playing all ones, until a preconfigured amount of data (usually half the jitter buffer) arrives or a timer expires. It then enters normal operation and performs clock recovery. Losing a preconfigured number of consecutive packets, or the timer expiring, moves it to a packet loss state, where it marks outgoing packets with the R bit.

It MAY detect defects: stray packets, malformed packets, excessive packet loss rate, buffer overrun and remote packet loss. Alarms are typically reported after 2.5 seconds and cleared after 10 seconds. Optional performance monitoring is derived following G.826.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver keeps a small waiting area so buckets can arrive a bit unevenly. If a bucket is missing, it pours in filler so the stream keeps flowing.

sections.title: QoS and Congestion Control
sections.content:
SAToP SHOULD use the QoS features of the underlying PSN, such as a Diffserv per-domain behavior with low jitter and low loss, or Intserv Guaranteed Service with a bandwidth reservation at least equal to the aggregate TDM traffic.

SAToP pseudowires are inelastic constant bit-rate flows and cannot respond to congestion in a TCP-friendly way. They SHOULD be carried across traffic-engineered PSNs where possible, and SAToP IP packets SHOULD NOT use the default DSCP value. Over a best-effort PSN, a pseudowire SHOULD monitor packet loss to detect severe congestion and, if detected, SHOULD shut down bi-directionally for a period. The exact criteria for severe congestion are left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: A steady stream cannot slow down when the road is jammed, so it is best sent on roads with reserved lanes.

sections.title: Security and Applicability
sections.content:
SAToP neither enhances nor detracts from the security of the underlying PSN and relies on PSN mechanisms for encryption, integrity and authentication. SRTP is NOT RECOMMENDED as a substitute for pseudowire layer security. Random initial sequence numbers make known-plaintext attacks on encrypted pseudowires harder, and misconnection detection adds resilience to misconfiguration and some denial-of-service attacks.

The applicability statement is candid about limits. TDM streams may see more delay than native TDM, from packetization, the PSN and the jitter buffer. The service is sensitive to packet loss, and replacement data only prevents shutting down the interface on occasional loss, not errored blocks. Structure-aware emulation (CESoPSN or TDMoIP) can completely hide packet loss effects from the customer. SAToP provides no mechanism for protection against PSN outages, though loss replacement and reordering help with fast rerouting.
sections.plainLanguage: SAToP leaves locking the boxes to the delivery network. It also admits that lost buckets cause some trouble that cannot be hidden.

fields.name: Zero bits
fields.desc: Set to zero unless starting an Associated Channel Header.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: TDM data is invalid due to an attachment circuit fault.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Local CE-bound IWF is in the packet loss state.

fields.name: RSV
fields.desc: Reserved; set to 0 and ignored by receiver.

fields.name: LEN
fields.desc: Packet length if under 64 bytes, otherwise zero.

fields.name: Sequence number
fields.desc: 16-bit circular sequence number with a random start.
